Greenfield.metaTitle: Wildlife Removal in Greenfield, MA | Franklin County Pros
Greenfield.metaDescription: Raccoon, bat, and skunk removal in Greenfield, MA. Homes near Poet's Seat Tower and the Green River, plus same-day service — call our crew.
Greenfield.housing_era: Greenfield, the Franklin County seat, has dense early-1900s colonials, triple-deckers, and multifamily homes near downtown, with postwar capes and ranches in the outer neighborhoods. Older housing near the rivers has stone foundations and aging rooflines that wildlife exploits.

Greenfield.wildlife_intro:
Greenfield sits where the Green River meets the Connecticut, under the wooded Rocky Mountain ridge, and its housing takes pressure from all three. Raccoons and gray squirrels are constant in the older colonials and multifamily homes, bats roost in attics near the rivers, and skunks and opossums den under porches throughout the in-town neighborhoods. Woodchucks work the garden lots and sunny banks, and beavers on the Green River and local brooks occasionally flood low properties on the edges of town.

Franklin County winters push animals indoors early, and spring denning season fills chimneys with raccoon families. Our crew inspects the full structure, removes animals on site as Massachusetts law requires, and seals entry points so the fix lasts. Every job is handled by a MassWildlife-licensed Problem Animal Control agent. If you hear thumping in the attic at night or smell skunk under the porch more than once, call us and we will come out and assess it.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost here?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much exclusion and cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts. Simple one-animal jobs cost less than bat exclusion or attic cleanup after a long stay. Call us for an assessment of your home.

faqs.q: There is a skunk living under my Greenfield porch — what are my options?
faqs.a: Skunks denning under porches are common in Greenfield's older neighborhoods. A licensed Problem Animal Control agent can trap the skunk and handle it on site under Massachusetts rules, and we recommend screening the porch opening with buried hardware cloth afterward so the sheltered space does not attract the next animal.

Montague.wildlife_intro:
Montague wraps around a bend of the Connecticut River and includes the mill village of Turners Falls, the Millers Falls village on the Millers River, and wide rural stretches around the Montague Plains. Bats are a leading call in the mill housing, where old rooflines shelter summer colonies, and raccoons and squirrels follow the river corridors into attics across the villages. Skunks and opossums are common under porches, woodchucks work the fields and gardens, and beavers regularly dam brooks and culverts in the rural parts of town.

Our crew treats each village differently — a brick block in Turners Falls needs a different inspection than a farmhouse in Montague Center. We remove animals on site under Massachusetts law, seal the entry points, and, for beaver flooding, explain the permit route before any work begins. Call us for a straight assessment from a MassWildlife-licensed Problem Animal Control agent who knows these villages.

faqs.q: Beavers keep damming a culvert near my Montague home — what can be done?
faqs.a: Beaver work in Massachusetts is permit-framed: during the regular season a licensed Problem Animal Control agent can trap under permit, and off-season flooding usually needs a Board of Health emergency permit first. Sometimes a flow device protects the culvert without removing beavers. Our crew will inspect the site and lay out the lawful options.

Orange.wildlife_intro:
Orange sits on the Millers River in the eastern corner of Franklin County, surrounded by state forest and working farmland. Raccoons, gray squirrels, and bats are the core calls in the mill-era housing, where old foundations and rooflines offer easy entry. Skunks and opossums den under porches and barns, woodchucks are a fixture in the fields and gardens, and beavers work the Millers and Tully rivers and the brooks feeding Lake Mattawa, sometimes flooding roads and septic systems.

Much of our Orange work pairs removal with real sealing — trapping an animal out of a house with five open gaps accomplishes little. Our crew removes animals on site as Massachusetts law requires, then closes the entries we found. Seasonal cottages at Lake Mattawa get the same treatment so they sit tight over winter. Call us at the first scratching, odor, or droppings and a MassWildlife-licensed Problem Animal Control agent will inspect the place properly.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost here?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much exclusion and cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts. Simple one-animal jobs cost less than bat exclusion or attic cleanup after a long stay. Call us for an assessment of your home.

faqs.q: How do I know if the noise in my Orange attic is squirrels or a raccoon?
faqs.a: Squirrels are active at dawn and dusk and sound like quick scampering and rolling nuts, while raccoons are heavier, mostly nocturnal, and thump and drag. Droppings and entry-hole size confirm it. Our crew inspects free of guesswork — call us and we will identify the animal, remove it on site, and seal the entry.

Deerfield.metaDescription: Bat, raccoon, and woodchuck removal in Deerfield, MA. Colonial homes on The Street and Connecticut River farmland — same-day service, call us.
Deerfield.housing_era: Old Deerfield is one of New England's best-preserved colonial streets, with 1700s and 1800s homes along The Street, while South Deerfield has village housing, farmhouses, and newer homes spread across rich Connecticut River farmland. Historic houses have hand-hewn framing, old chimneys, and generations of additions.

Deerfield.wildlife_intro:
Deerfield pairs a museum-preserved colonial village with some of the richest farmland in the Pioneer Valley, all along the Connecticut River under the Pocumtuck Range. Bats are the signature call in the historic homes, where old chimneys and timber framing shelter colonies, and raccoons and squirrels are steady in the village and farm housing. Woodchucks are a serious garden and field-edge problem on the farms, skunks and opossums work the barns and porches, and beavers flood low ground along the Deerfield River and valley brooks.

Historic fabric changes how exclusion is done — our crew seals entry points with care for old materials and appearance, and removes animals on site under Massachusetts law. Bat work follows the state's tight windows, May 1–31 and August 1–October 15, and is exclusion-only. If your Deerfield home is hearing wings in the wall or finding guano in the attic, call us early so the work can be scheduled inside a legal window.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost here?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much exclusion and cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts. Simple one-animal jobs cost less than bat exclusion or attic cleanup after a long stay. Call us for an assessment of your home.

faqs.q: My historic Deerfield home has bats — can they be removed without harming the house?
faqs.a: Yes. Bat work in Massachusetts is exclusion-only: a licensed Problem Animal Control agent seals secondary gaps and fits one-way devices at the main exits, and it can only be done May 1–31 or August 1–October 15. On historic homes our crew uses reversible, low-profile sealing that protects old trim and masonry while closing the roost.

Sunderland.wildlife_intro:
Sunderland is a farming town on the Connecticut River under Mount Toby, minutes from UMass Amherst, and its calls reflect both sides of that life. Raccoons and bats move into farmhouses and barns along the river, gray squirrels and mice fill rentals and village homes, and woodchucks, skunks, and opossums work the fields, gardens, and outbuildings. Beavers dam the Sawmill River and valley brooks, and the Mount Toby forest keeps a steady supply of wildlife at the eastern doorsteps.

Barns deserve special attention here — a raccoon family or bat colony established in a barn often spreads to the house. Our crew inspects house and outbuildings together, removes animals on site under Massachusetts law, and seals what can be sealed. Student rentals benefit from a fall inspection before mice and squirrels settle in for winter. Call us and a MassWildlife-licensed Problem Animal Control agent will give you a clear plan for the whole property.

faqs.q: Woodchucks are eating our Sunderland garden and digging by the barn — can you stop it?

Northfield.wildlife_intro:
Northfield is a Connecticut River town at the top of Franklin County, with a historic Main Street, big former school buildings, and farms spread between the river and forested hills. Bats are common in the large older buildings and village homes, raccoons and gray squirrels work the attics along Main Street, and skunks, opossums, and woodchucks cover the farms and gardens. Beavers are a recurring issue on Pauchaug Brook and other wetlands, flooding fields, driveways, and culverts in the low parts of town.

The scale of the older buildings here means inspections need to be thorough — bats especially can use several exits across a large roofline. Our crew maps every entry point, removes animals on site under Massachusetts rules, and seals the structure in the right season. Beaver flooding is handled through the proper permits, which we will explain before starting. Call us for an honest assessment from a MassWildlife-licensed Problem Animal Control agent.
